sentences.text: Amurosaurus is distinguished by unique skull features and a distinctive S-shaped ulna bone.
Although the crest bones are missing, modified skull roof bones suggest Amurosaurus likely had a hollow crest like other lambeosaurines.
This duck-billed dinosaur is estimated to have reached a length of 8 meters and a weight of 3 metric tons.
This duck-billed dinosaur is the best-known dinosaur from Russia.
Amurosaurus had a high encephalisation quotient, suggesting it likely engaged in complex social behaviors.
Amurosaurus was first described and named by Russian paleontologists Yuri Bolotsky and Sergei Kurzanov in 1991.
Only one species, A. rabinini, is known, named in honor of Russian paleontologist Anatoly Rabinin who led the first Russian expeditions to the Amur region in 1916 and 1917.
All Amurosaurus fossils come from a single bonebed discovered in 1984 near Blagoveschensk in the Amur Oblast of Russia.
The holotype specimen consists of a left maxilla and a left dentary from the same individual.
Recent descriptions of additional material have made Amurosaurus the most abundant and completely known dinosaur from Russia.
As a hadrosaurid, Amurosaurus was a herbivore.
Many tooth marks on the bones were made by predators or scavengers, indicating frequent interaction with carnivores.

Sediments indicate an alluvial plain and river transported the fossils only a short distance, as evidenced by disarticulated and randomly ordered but well-preserved bones, including fragile skull elements.
Amurosaurus is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Amurosaurus belongs to the family Hadrosauridae.
The parent group of Amurosaurus is Lambeosaurinae.
The genus Sahaliyania is considered a junior synonym of Amurosaurus.
A 2022 reassessment confirmed that Sahaliyania is a junior synonym of Amurosaurus.

Due to the recent description of most of its unique features, in early 2006 Amurosaurus was included in a cladistic analysis placing it as a basal member of the hadrosaurid subfamily Lambeosaurinae, but more derived than Tsintaosaurus or Jaxartosaurus.
Amurosaurus lived in eastern Asia during the Late Cretaceous, between 70 and 66 million years ago.
The fossils date to the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 68 million years ago.
The formation dates to the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 74 to 66 million years ago, though there is some disagreement about the exact timing of deposition.
Amurosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
All known basal lambeosaurines come from Asia, leading to the hypothesis that they originated there and later dispersed across the Bering Strait to North America.
Since members of both groups are found in North America and Asia, there must have been additional dispersal after their evolution, though the direction of that dispersal remains somewhat confusing.
